title: You’re Calling It Discernment, but You Haven’t Said One Kind Thing About Anyone in Months.
paragraphs: You’re Calling It Discernment, but You Haven’t Said One Kind Thing About Anyone in Months.
Maybe the frightening question isn’t whether you can recognize what is wrong with everyone else. Maybe it’s what constantly looking for what is wrong has been doing to your own heart.
You saw the sermon clip and immediately noticed the theological weakness.
You read the Christian post and found the sentence that bothered you.
Someone shared a testimony, and before you could rejoice that a broken person was reaching toward Jesus, your mind started examining everything they said incorrectly.
A pastor preached.
You analyzed him.
A worship leader sang.
You questioned her motives.
A Christian fell publicly.
You watched.
Another ministry made a decision you disagreed with.
You posted about it.
Someone tried to encourage believers, and within seconds you were scrolling through the comments looking for somebody who would say what you were already thinking:
“Finally. Someone with discernment.”
And maybe sometimes you were right.
That is what makes this so dangerous.
Because error really exists.
False teaching really exists.
Hypocrisy really exists.
Manipulation really exists.

The Bible actually commands believers to test what they hear. Jesus warned about false prophets. Paul confronted destructive teaching. John told Christians not to believe every spirit but to test the spirits. Jude urged believers to contend for the faith.
Biblical discernment is real.
Necessary, even.
But there is another question we rarely ask:
What if you became so good at identifying what is wrong that you slowly lost the ability to rejoice in what is good?
What if somewhere between “testing everything” and “calling everything out,” your heart changed?
What if what you have been calling discernment has quietly become cynicism?
Because there is something unsettling about a Christian who can find something wrong with almost everyone but cannot remember the last time they spoke generously about anyone.
Paul gives us a startling diagnostic in Philippians 4:8.
The Greek text reads:
“Τὸ λοιπόν, ἀδελφοί, ὅσα ἐστὶν ἀληθῆ, ὅσα σεμνά, ὅσα δίκαια, ὅσα ἁγνά, ὅσα προσφιλῆ, ὅσα εὔφημα, εἴ τις ἀρετὴ καὶ εἴ τις ἔπαινος, ταῦτα λογίζεσθε.”

“Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable—if there is any excellence and if there is anything worthy of praise—think about these things.”
That last expression matters.
“ταῦτα λογίζεσθε” — tauta logizesthe.
Think on these things.
Consider them.
Take them into account.
Let your mind deliberately dwell upon them.
Paul is not teaching naïveté.
He is not commanding Christians to pretend evil is good.
He is not telling the church to abandon doctrinal vigilance, tolerate deception, or smile politely while wolves destroy sheep.
He is describing a mind increasingly governed by Christ.
And that means biblical discernment cannot merely ask:
“What is false?”
It must also recognize:
“What is true?”
Not merely:
“What is corrupt?”
But:
“What is pure?”
Not merely:
“What deserves correction?”
But:
“What is worthy of praise?”
That may expose something uncomfortable in us.
When was the last time you praised something good in another believer without immediately adding a qualification?
When was the last time another Christian succeeded and you celebrated without secretly wondering whether they deserved it?
When was the last time someone preached Christ faithfully and you thanked God instead of searching for the three sentences you would have worded differently?
When was the last time you looked at another struggling believer and saw someone Jesus loves rather than another theological problem waiting to be diagnosed?
Some of us have become spiritually fluent in criticism.
We know the vocabulary.
“Discernment.”
“Compromise.”
“Deception.”
“Lukewarm.”
“False teacher.”
“Wolf.”
“Heretic.”
“Worldly.”
“Unbiblical.”
And again—those categories can sometimes be necessary.
Scripture itself contains severe warnings.
But possessing biblical vocabulary does not automatically mean we possess a biblical heart.
You can quote verses about wolves while becoming cruel to sheep.
You can defend sound doctrine while speaking with an unsound spirit.
You can expose another person’s pride while feeding your own.
You can become so addicted to being the person who “sees through everything” that suspicion becomes part of your identity.
Then something frightening happens.
Grace starts irritating you.
Mercy feels suspicious.
Gentleness sounds weak.
Patience looks like compromise.
And anyone who refuses to be as angry as you are begins looking spiritually immature.
Meanwhile, you feel increasingly righteous because you are increasingly offended.
But anger is not automatically holiness.
Suspicion is not automatically wisdom.
Criticism is not automatically courage.
And cynicism wearing a Bible verse is still cynicism.
Jesus Christ was never morally confused.
Nobody possessed greater discernment.
He saw hypocrisy so clearly that religious pretenders could not hide behind robes, titles, prayers, or public reputations.
Jesus called some religious leaders “whitewashed tombs.”
He overturned tables.
He confronted sin.
He warned about judgment.
He never diluted truth to make rebellion comfortable.
And yet...
Children wanted to approach Him.
Broken people came near Him.
The disgraced found themselves talking to Him.
A woman with a scandalous reputation could weep at His feet.
A tax collector could climb down from a tree and discover that salvation had come to his house.
A thief dying beside Him could turn his head toward Jesus with almost nothing left except desperate faith and hear words of hope.
How could the holiest Man who ever walked this earth be uncompromising toward sin and yet magnetic to broken sinners?
Because holiness and cruelty are not synonyms.
Truth and lovelessness are not twins.
Jesus did not need cynicism to remain discerning.
Neither do we.
Perhaps this is where the knife reaches deeper.
Maybe your criticism began somewhere understandable.
Someone deceived you.
A church hurt you.
A leader disappointed you.
A Christian you trusted lived a double life.
You believed somebody who should have protected you, and instead they wounded you.
So you learned to inspect everything.
At first, it felt like wisdom.
Never again.
Never trust too quickly.
Never be fooled.
Never lower your guard.
You started spotting inconsistencies before anyone else noticed them.
That vigilance protected you from being naïve again.
But eventually the shield became a prison.
You stopped merely discerning danger.
You started expecting it.
You stopped examining fruit.
You started assuming motives.
You stopped asking whether something was true.
You began assuming there must be something wrong somewhere.
And slowly...
almost imperceptibly...
you became difficult to impress but easy to offend.
Hard to deceive, perhaps.
But also hard to encourage.
Hard to teach.
Hard to surprise with goodness.
Maybe even hard to love.
This is where the Gospel confronts us.
Not merely “those people.”
Us.
Me.
You.
Because the Gospel destroys our fantasy that we are standing above humanity grading everyone else's righteousness.
At the foot of the cross, there are no professional spectators.
There are sinners.
Every one of us arrives guilty.
Every one of us needs mercy.
Every one of us has thoughts we would never want projected onto a screen.
Every one of us has spoken words we wish we could retrieve.
Every one of us has failed to love God perfectly and failed to love our neighbor as ourselves.
And yet Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we could not produce.
He bore sin on the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Grace does not tell us sin does not matter.
The cross proves precisely how seriously God takes sin.
Grace tells us something even more astonishing:
Sin does not get the final word for the person who comes to Christ.
Jesus does.
That changes how we see people.
Because suddenly the person you are criticizing is no longer merely “that hypocrite.”
They are a human being who needs Christ.
The person whose theology is confused is not merely content for your next angry post.
They are a soul.
The believer who stumbled is not entertainment.
They are someone for whom restoration may still be possible.
And the person who needs repentance?
Yes, tell the truth.
But remember what repentance is for.
Restoration to God.
We are not supposed to expose darkness because we enjoy watching people bleed.
We expose darkness because we love the Light.
There is a difference.
A massive one.
Biblical discernment grieves when someone falls.
Cynicism feels vindicated.
Discernment wants error corrected.
Cynicism wants the offender humiliated.
Discernment can say, “This teaching is wrong,” without secretly enjoying the destruction of the person teaching it.
Cynicism needs villains because villains make cynics feel righteous.
Discernment examines evidence.
Cynicism assumes motives.
Discernment remains teachable.
Cynicism becomes convinced that nearly everyone else is compromised.
Discernment protects the church.
Cynicism eventually poisons it.
James gives us another uncomfortable mirror:
“But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits...” (James 3:17).
Read that again.
“Full of mercy.”
Not empty of conviction.
Not indifferent to truth.
Full of mercy.
If your version of spiritual wisdom has made mercy nearly impossible, something has gone wrong.
Paul says in Ephesians 4:15 that believers are to speak “the truth in love.”
Truth matters.
Love matters.
Remove truth, and love becomes sentimental indulgence.
Remove love, and truth can become a weapon for self-exaltation.
Christ gives us neither counterfeit.
He gives us truth saturated with holy love.
Maybe you need to examine your recent conversations.
Your comments.
Your reposts.
Your private messages.
Your church conversations after Sunday service.
Your social-media history.
Imagine somebody knew nothing about Christianity except what they saw you consistently emphasize.
Would they conclude Christianity is primarily about Jesus Christ crucified and risen for sinners?
Or would they conclude Christianity is mostly about identifying everybody who is doing Christianity incorrectly?
That question hurts.
It is supposed to.
Not because God delights in condemning His children, but because conviction can be mercy.
Maybe the Holy Spirit is showing you something before bitterness hardens further.
Maybe beneath the word “discernment” there is resentment.
Maybe beneath the constant criticism there is pride.
Maybe beneath the suspicion there is unresolved church hurt.
Maybe you discovered that finding faults gives you something intoxicating:
the feeling of superiority.
You see what they cannot see.
You know what they do not know.
You would never make their mistake.
You would never compromise like that.
You would never fall like them.
Be careful.
Peter once believed he knew exactly what Peter would never do.
Then a rooster crowed.
And the man who insisted he would die beside Jesus discovered that under pressure he could deny even knowing Him.
Yet Peter's scandal was not the end of Peter's story.
Jesus restored him.
That is our theme because it is woven throughout the Gospel:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming rebellion righteousness.
Not by lowering God's holiness.
Jesus rewrites ruined stories through repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and transforming grace.
Peter failed.
Jesus restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Jesus transformed him.
The thief was dying under judgment for his crimes.
Jesus gave him hope beyond the grave.
Again and again, Scripture refuses to let a person's darkest chapter automatically become their final chapter.
So why are we sometimes so eager to do what Jesus did not?
Why do we freeze people inside their worst moment?
Why do we sometimes remember another Christian's failure more faithfully than we remember Christ's power to restore?
There are situations where boundaries remain necessary.
Consequences can remain.
Trust may need to be rebuilt.
Church discipline is biblical.
False teaching must sometimes be publicly corrected.
Abuse should never be concealed beneath cheap language about forgiveness.
Forgiveness does not mean calling evil good, and mercy does not require abandoning wisdom.
But even when correction is necessary, Christians do not receive permission to feast on another person's destruction.
Our enemy is not entertained when Christians become discerning.
He is threatened by it.
But he is perfectly capable of exploiting something that begins as discernment and twisting it into pride, bitterness, suspicion, and contempt.
So perhaps the question tonight is painfully simple.
When was the last time you said something kind about another believer?
Not flattering.
Not fake.
Kind.
When was the last time you saw something honorable and said so?
When was the last time you deliberately looked for something “true... honorable... just... pure... lovely... commendable,” as Philippians 4:8 commands?
When was the last time someone else received praise and you didn't feel the need to remind everybody of their flaws?
When was the last time you prayed for the person you were tempted to publicly destroy?
That might be the test.
Before posting about them...
pray for them.
Before assuming their motives...
remember that God sees motives perfectly and you do not.
Before celebrating their collapse...
remember Peter.
Before declaring someone beyond restoration...
remember Paul.
Before staring too long at another person's scandal...
remember yours.
And then remember Jesus.
Maybe you have spent months examining everyone except yourself.
Maybe this article irritated you before it convicted you.
Maybe you already began constructing arguments against it while reading.
Fine.
Take those arguments to Scripture.
Test everything written here.
Biblical discernment demands nothing less.
But also ask Jesus the question cynicism desperately avoids:
“Lord, is there anything in me that needs to change?”
Then be quiet long enough for the answer.
Because repentance is not humiliation before an audience.
Repentance is an invitation home.
If you recognize yourself here, don't hide behind another theological argument.
Come to Christ.
Confess the pride.
Confess the bitterness.
Confess the secret pleasure you have sometimes felt when someone you disliked finally fell.
Confess the way criticism became easier than prayer.
Confess the way suspicion replaced love.
There is grace for this too.
Jesus did not go to the cross only for the sins you find socially embarrassing.
He died for pride.
For bitterness.
For self-righteousness.
For loveless speech.
For secret contempt.
For religious arrogance.
For all the darkness we become skilled at recognizing in everybody except ourselves.
And He still saves.
He still forgives.
He still restores.
He still transforms.
He can make a cynical heart tender without making it gullible.
He can make a discerning Christian gracious without making them compromising.
He can teach you to recognize a wolf while still loving the sheep.
He can teach you to confront error without becoming addicted to confrontation.
He can teach you to speak truth without forgetting that the people hearing it are souls.
That is maturity.
Not seeing evil everywhere.
Seeing everything through the lordship of Jesus Christ.
If this exposed something you have been hiding behind the word “discernment,” be honest.
Not for performance.
Not because typing a sentence saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that God is dealing with us breaks the strange power of pretending we have everybody figured out except ourselves.
Let other believers know there is a real person behind the screen who needs prayer, grace, and restoration too.
If you know someone whose Christian life has slowly become consumed by criticism, don't send this to them like ammunition.
Send it with love.
Better yet, read it again for yourself first.
Because the next time outrage feels spiritually satisfying, you may need Philippians 4:8 again.
It does not.
But if you genuinely want to glorify God by helping Gospel-centered truth reach more people, supporting faithful Christian ministry can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership.
Send it privately to someone who has been wounded into cynicism.
Because somewhere tonight there is a Christian who thinks bitterness means they are discerning.
Someone thinks suspicion means they are wise.
Someone has been hurt so badly by church people that they no longer know how to look at another believer without searching for the knife.
Maybe they need correction.
Maybe they need healing.
Maybe they need both.
But more than another argument...
they need Jesus.
And perhaps so do we.
Because eventually discernment must do more than recognize darkness.
It must recognize the Light.
And when you have spent enough time looking at Jesus, you may discover something terrifying and beautiful:
The closer you get to the only truly righteous Man who ever lived, the less interested you become in pretending you are the righteous one in the room.
Never become so skilled at finding what is wrong with everyone else that you forget what grace did with everything that was wrong with you.
